facts.title: Known Since Antiquity
facts.text: Sulfur is one of a handful of elements known since prehistoric times, with no single discoverer. The Bible refers to it as "brimstone" (literally "burning stone"), and Egyptians used it for bleaching cloth thousands of years ago. In 1777 Antoine Lavoisier finally proved it was a true chemical element rather than a compound.

facts.title: Why It Is Spelled "Sulfur"
facts.text: The name derives from the Latin "sulphur," itself possibly rooted in a Sanskrit word for fire. In 1990 the IUPAC officially adopted "sulfur" with an f as the international standard spelling, and the British Royal Society of Chemistry followed in 1992. The older "sulphur" spelling is now considered traditional rather than correct in scientific writing.

facts.title: It Powers Global Industry
facts.text: More sulfuric acid (H2SO4) is produced than any other industrial chemical on Earth, with hundreds of millions of tonnes made each year. A nation's sulfuric acid output is often used as a rough index of its industrial strength. The bulk of it goes into making phosphate fertilizers that feed much of the world's agriculture.

facts.title: A Champion of Allotropes
facts.text: Sulfur forms more allotropes (different structural forms) than almost any other element, with more than 30 known. Its most stable form at room temperature is orthorhombic alpha-sulfur, built from crown-shaped rings of eight atoms (S8). When you melt and heat these rings further they break and tangle, which is why molten sulfur strangely gets more viscous as it gets hotter before thinning out again.

facts.title: Essential to Your Body
facts.text: Sulfur is the eighth most abundant element in the human body and is vital to life. It sits inside the amino acids cysteine and methionine, and the disulfide bonds it forms hold proteins like keratin in your hair and nails into their shapes. This same chemistry is why burning hair smells so distinctly of sulfur.

facts.title: Volcanoes and Yellow Lakes
facts.text: Sulfur often occurs in pure native form around volcanoes and hot springs, where it crystallizes into vivid yellow deposits. At Indonesia's Kawah Ijen volcano, miners famously carry heavy baskets of solid sulfur out of a crater that also glows with eerie blue flames of burning sulfur gas at night. Underground deposits were historically mined by the Frasch process, which melts sulfur with superheated water and pumps it to the surface.

facts.title: It Built the Sky of Venus
facts.text: Sulfur is widespread in the cosmos and dramatically shapes other worlds. The thick clouds of Venus are made largely of sulfuric acid droplets, and Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, painted yellow, orange, and red by sulfur compounds erupting from its surface. Sulfur is forged in massive stars and scattered by supernova explosions.

facts.title: The Spark in Gunpowder
facts.text: Sulfur is one of the three classic ingredients of black powder, alongside charcoal and potassium nitrate (saltpeter). It lowers the temperature needed to ignite the mixture and helps the reaction spread quickly, which is why this combination revolutionized warfare and later powered fireworks. The same readiness to burn is why ancient writers called it brimstone.

facts.title: Vulcanizing Rubber Changed the World
facts.text: In 1839 Charles Goodyear discovered that heating natural rubber with sulfur transformed it from a sticky, temperature-sensitive material into the tough, springy substance we use today. The sulfur atoms form cross-links between the rubber's polymer chains, a process now called vulcanization. Without it there would be no durable car tires, and the Goodyear tire company is named in his honor.

facts.title: Medicine, Old and New
facts.text: Sulfur has a long medical history, from ancient skin treatments to the sulfonamides ("sulfa drugs") of the 1930s, the first widely effective antibacterial medicines that saved countless lives before penicillin. Sulfur-containing compounds remain important in many modern drugs and in fungicides for crops. It also occurs naturally in garlic and onions, where sulfur compounds create their pungent flavors and make your eyes water.
